title: Weekly POC sync — error patterns, throttling, and mitigation

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-12 15:00 PST / Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood SE), Priya (QuantaLogix ML), Lucas (QuantaLogix Platform), Marta (QuantaLogix CTO)
Links shared: redwood bench spreadsheet (short): https://redwood.app/bench/qlx-poc , SOC2 packet (REDWOOD-SOC2-SEP25)

00:00:05 Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — surface what happened friday night, walk root cause, immediate mitigations, and next steps.
00:00:18 Marta: thanks Ava. yeah that 3am spike was painful — customer-facing errors. wanted to understand the "why" and ensure we don't hit that in peak next week.
00:00:28 Jonah: yeah hi, i'll start with a quick recap of what we saw. we observed two correlated phenomena: a sudden increase in 5xx (mostly 503/504) and a concurrent rise in tail latency for a subset of routes. logs indicate many retries from your client which exacerbated load.
00:00:50 Priya: we saw about 0.9% 5xx during the peak window but it clustered into two 8-minute bursts. most requests were mid-sized prompts — 800 to 1600 token windows.
00:01:05 Samir: just to clarify — are these 503s from the gateway or from the model runner? our trace shows origin as the runner hitting circuit-breaker timeouts then returning 503 up the chain. some transcriptions flagged as 5-0-3 but yeah 503s.
00:01:23 Lucas: the client's SDK automatically retried on 500s, default backoff, so we had an amplification effect.
00:01:35 Jonah: exactly. initial trigger appears to be batch sizing hitting a bad sweet spot — with your traffic mix we had a few large batches that pushed sequence length long and caused per-token compute blowouts. that plus autoscaler lag — we didn't have enough warm GPUs for the sudden token inflate so the runner hit queue-length thresholds and returned 503s.
00:02:00 Priya: when you say "batch sizing" are you referring to the runtime continuous batching? we didn't change anything on our end.
00:02:09 Jonah: yes — Redwood runtime aggregates concurrently arriving requests into batches to improve throughput. normally that's fine, but when one request has a long context it inflates the whole batch. we saw long-tail tokenization (one request with 8k tokens) that spiked kernel time. also the KV cache (or kv cash in some early logs) was cold for several embeddings because of a restart — so cache misses exacerbated compute.
00:02:37 Priya: oh — 8k? our instrumented client shouldn't be hitting that, i'll double-check. maybe a bug in prompt generation created an accidental full-history append.
00:02:49 Ava: Okay — so hypothesized chain is: large/aberrant request -> large batch -> long per-token time -> autoscaler lag -> queue growth -> gateway timeouts and 503 -> client retries -> amplification. Does that match?
00:03:03 Jonah: yes. plus we noticed rate-limiter behavior: when the system returned 429s it behaved differently than when returning 503; your SDK's retry logic treats 429 with immediate retry vs 5xx with exponential backoff and that mismatch changed the shape of the load.
00:03:20 Lucas: our SDK retry config is default — i think it retries 2x for 429 immediately. we'll need to change that.
00:03:28 Samir: quick note — some of the transcription of our debug logs flagged "Redwood Dedicate" which is just transcription errors for Redwood Dedicated. ignore that.
00:03:37 Marta: SOC2/questions — while we triage this, can you confirm logs and audit trail will be preserved for our compliance?
00:03:46 Ava: yes — we have retention on the pilot for 90 days and we can export full traces; i'll send SOC2 packet after this call.
00:03:56 Priya: one more detail — we saw 504 gateway timeouts mostly on async routes that call an internal reranker. maybe chaining contributed.
00:04:07 Jonah: yep chaining increases end-to-end time and multiplies opportunities for queues. reranking calls were causing an extra 200ms p99 addition.

00:05:00 Jonah: i'll walk through logs we pulled. (screen share ref) initial spike timeline: 02:12 - 02:20 UTC two large bursts. CPU cycles scaled up slowly — autoscale policy uses 60s window and then a warm-up delay, so there was a 45–90s lag to spin up extra VMs. by then the queued requests hit profile-based circuit breakers which return 503.
00:05:29 Priya: got it. is there a way to tune the autoscaler to be more aggressive for these routes? we have a windowed traffic spike pattern.
00:05:37 Jonah: yes. options: reduce scaling cooldown, enable burst capacity (reserved warm nodes) for the pilot, or use concurrency-based scaling rather than CPU-only. short-term we usually enable a small dedicated reserve of 1 GPU for peak windows.
00:05:52 Lucas: can we set burst reserve for only the specific model route? we have constraints on costs.
00:05:57 Samir: yep per-route pools are supported on Dedicated; for hosted we can create a route config to favor warm instances for that model id. that costs a bit but is cheaper than outage.

00:06:30 Marta: what about changing client retry behavior? seems like low-effort mitigation.
00:06:36 Jonah: absolutely. set 429 to use a jittered exponential backoff, and cap retries. for 5xx prefer exponential with larger initial backoff (200-500ms). avoid immediate retry on 429 as that encourages a thundering herd.
00:06:50 Priya: we'll push a fix to the SDK to change the 429 behavior.

00:07:10 Ava: any thoughts about prefix/KV cache warmup? i remember earlier in the pilot we saw cold starts after restarts.
00:07:17 Jonah: yes — if KV cache is empty and many requests rely on cached embeddings for prefix, then each request incurs extra embedding compute. we saw a restart event around 01:55 UTC which invalidated local node cache. solution: pre-warm cache on deploy, or use shared cache layer. also reduce expensive prefix recomputation by adding a short TTL for prefixes.
00:07:45 Priya: pre-warm sounds reasonable. is there an API or script to warm caches?
00:07:51 Samir: we can provide a 'cache warm' script and a small tool to replay representative prompts at low rate to fill local cache before route goes live. we'll include that in the artifact we share.

00:08:30 Jonah: another observation: batch size algorithm uses recent token length distribution. when a single large request appears it temporarily biases batch selection. we can cap per-batch token budget or split large requests at the gateway.
00:08:48 Lucas: splitting large requests — is that supported without breaking context? some of our prompts need full history.
00:08:55 Jonah: right — dangerous for strict-context use cases. instead we can enforce request size limits and fail-fast for oversized requests, or route oversized ones to a separate quota-limited pool.

00:09:20 Priya: what's the runway for implementing those mitigations? some are config flips? others need code.
00:09:28 Samir: timeline: client retry changes — low effort, your devs can patch in hours. apply temporary route rate cap — a few minutes via console. enable burst reserve — needs account config but we can do it within a day. cache warm scripts + load test — SE will deliver in 48–72 hours. longer work like batch algorithm changes will be a product/eng ticket.

00:10:02 Jonah: for immediate mitigation tonight we recommend: (1) set conservative client retry config, (2) apply a temporary soft rate limit for suspect route to 300 rps, (3) enable a 1-GPU warm reserve on the route for peak hours, (4) run a 90m load test to validate.
00:10:20 Priya: that seems fine. we'll make client changes and apply rate limit in staging today.

00:11:05 Ava: quick commercial question — if we need a day or two of warm reserve on Dedicated, how will that show in pilot billing?
00:11:14 Jonah: we can offer a discounted pilot reserve rate for short windows; Ava will follow up with pricing note.

00:12:00 Lucas: also, a gotcha — some of our observability shows lots of small failed HTTP connections earlier; could network transient be involved?
00:12:09 Samir: possible — we correlated BGP flaps with one cluster but primary driver still appears compute. we'll keep monitoring.

00:13:20 Priya: what about 429 semantics — can Redwood include explanatory headers to tell us more about the bucket (x-rate-limit, retry-after)?
00:13:28 Jonah: yes we already emit headers but we can add more detail: bucket-id and current-usage for debugging — non-prod only. we typically avoid exposing production bucket internals in headers for security, but for pilot debugging we can enable detailed headers on a per-account basis.

00:14:05 Marta: any security/compliance impact from enabling more verbose headers?
00:14:11 Ava: minimal; it's metadata about rate usage but we can gate it behind SSO.

00:15:00 Jonah: i'll summarize root causes and mitigations in writing and attach logs. (Jonah posts link to raw log bundle)
00:15:10 Priya: thanks. can you also include the 5xx stack traces? some of our engineers wanted to see the exact kernel failure.
00:15:17 Jonah: yup will include stack traces and kernel time histograms.

00:16:40 Lucas: about retries — do you have recommended parameters? we run the open-source SDK with default.
00:16:47 Samir: recommended: for 429 -> retry 3x with initial backoff 300 ms and jitter; for 5xx -> retry 2x with initial backoff 500 ms and exponential factor 2; max total retry time cap 5s. avoid sync immediate retries for 429.
00:17:10 Priya: we'll adopt that.

00:18:00 Jonah: now, on monitoring — set Alert if 5xx > 0.5% for 5 minutes and p99 latency > 2s. also trace sampling increase for suspect route to 50% for two hours after deploy so we can correlate.
00:18:16 Ava: we'll share recommended alert thresholds in the post-call note.

00:20:00 Jonah: we'll also run a synthetic steady-state + spike test which will: warm cache, then ramp to baseline 200 rps, then inject a 2-minute spike to 800 rps and observe. we'll capture p50/p90/p99 and 5xx rate.
00:20:22 Priya: makes sense. please include the test script so we can reproduce on our side.

00:22:00 Marta: hypothetically, if we need to go private/VPC for compliance, would that change the scaling dynamics?
00:22:09 Jonah: yes, private deployments give more control over autoscale policies and node sizing; warm reserve patterns are easier since you control the infra. but setup time and cost are longer. we'll discuss if needed.

00:24:00 Ava: recap of commitments: Jonah will run the load test and share logs; Priya/Lucas will share request histograms and change retry settings; Ava will send SOC2 + pricing; Samir will provide cache warm script and preliminary per-route rate headers for debugging.
00:24:25 Priya: one more ask — can you surface which exact model variant was involved — we saw model-id redwood-v1-large in traces but some transcription shows redwood-v1-lrge.
00:24:36 Jonah: it was redwood-v1-large quantized 4-bit variant. we'll annotate traces with exact model hash.

00:25:00 (brief silence/typing)
00:26:12 Lucas: question — is there tooling to simulate client retries in the load test? it'd be good to see retry amplification effects.
00:26:20 Jonah: yes the SE load harness can simulate client retry policies and jitter. we'll include a flag to replicate your SDK defaults vs recommended.

00:28:00 Priya: any notable differences if we route oversized requests to a separate low-concurrency pool?
00:28:07 Samir: it reduces tail impact on the main pool but adds cost and potential higher latency for the oversized requests. tradeoff: isolation vs cost. often useful for rare large requests.

00:30:00 Jonah: i'm going to log a product ticket to evaluate batch-capping heuristics (prevent single request from inflating full-batch token budget). long-term fix, estimated prioritization TBD.
00:30:15 Ava: good. can we get the ticket id?
00:30:19 Jonah: i'll add it to the follow-up email.

00:31:00 Priya: one last operational ask — do you support per-route canary/fallback to smaller model variant automatically?
00:31:08 Samir: yes, route-level fallback is supported; you can configure an A/B where large requests get directed to a cheaper slower model, or to a smaller context. that's a config we can help set up.

00:33:50 Ava: ok folks, any other blockers?
00:33:55 Priya: none from me. thanks everyone.
00:34:05 Marta: please be explicit in the email about what we need to change in our client and where to flip the staging rate-limiter.
00:34:12 Ava: will do.
00:34:30 Jonah: i'll attach the load test script, log bundle, and stack traces.
00:34:40 Ava: great — thanks for the quick sync. we'll reconvene if the 90m test surfaces issues; otherwise next weekly is same time.
00:34:50 Lucas: thanks.
00:34:55 Samir: thanks all.
00:35:00 (call ends — post-call 12m of follow-up typing and note-sharing captured but not transcribed)
